claims.claim: The Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity (Latin: Passio sanctarum Perpetuae et Felicitatis) is a composite work that incorporates the writings of three authors: Perpetua, Saturus, and an anonymous editor called the Redactor.
Perpetua's first-person account (chapters 3–10) covers her arrest and imprisonment for her Christian faith and four visions she had in custody.
The Redactor's frame consists of a preface (chapters 1–2), a transition at 11.1, and an epilogue (chapters 14–21) describing the deaths of the martyrs, and the Redactor claims to be an eyewitness.
The Redactor adds a preface promoting his own theological view of the martyrs' stories.
The Redactor's identity is unknown; he was long thought to be Tertullian (ca. 150–220 CE), and one reviewer says a framework 'perhaps by Tertullian' is possible, but this attribution is uncertain.
The martyrs died in a North African amphitheater in the early third century, probably in Carthage on 7 March 203.
The text was most probably written in the first decade of the 3rd century, probably in Carthage.

According to the text, those arrested were the young catechumens Revocatus, his fellow slave Felicity, Saturninus, Secundulus, and Vibia Perpetua, who was well born, well educated and honourably married, with an infant son, and was about twenty-two years old.

Felicity was an enslaved woman who did not write any part of the work; her name in the title probably reflects her prominence in the narrative (she fears her pregnancy might prevent her execution) and the shared feast day of March 7.
